An AI consultant helps businesses identify where AI can solve problems, recommends the right tools, builds or implements solutions, and helps the business get measurable results.

You’re not just learning to use ChatGPT. You’re

There are different paths you can take:

• AI automation consultant
• AI strategy consultant

Some roles require coding and engineering experience. Others focus more on business strategy,

Step 1: Learn the fundamentals.

Understand how generative AI and large language models work, their limitations, hallucinations, data privacy and responsible use.

Learn how to evaluate AI outputs instead of accepting everything a tool produces.

Step 3: Learn practical AI tools.

Start with tools such as ChatGPT or Claude, then explore automation platforms like Make, Zapier or n8n.

Learn how to connect tools, build workflows, process information and introduce human review where necessary.

You don’t need to master every

Step 5: Learn to measure business results.

Can your solution save staff time? Reduce manual work? Improve the quality of customer support? Help a team process information faster?

Measure the results rather than making claims you cannot prove, You should also understand

Step 7: Get practical experience.

Offer to solve a clearly defined problem for a small business, build a demonstration project or collaborate with a team implementing AI.

Start with a manageable project, document the outcome and use that experience to approach other clients.

1. Start with the role, not the CV.

Before editing your CV, identify the 2–3 roles you actually want.

Search those exact titles on LinkedIn and job boards.

Open 20–30 recent vacancies and look for repeated requirements.

• Skills companies keep

2. Create a master CV but don’t send it everywhere.

Your master CV is your career inventory.

Keep all your relevant experience, projects, achievements, responsibilities, tools, certifications, training and measurable results in one document.

It can be 3–5 pages. That’s fine.

3. Quantify your work properly.

Numbers aren’t only revenue.

You can quantify:

• Number of people supported
• Applications screened
• Clients managed
• Projects completed
• Reports produced
• Candidates recruited
• Content published
• Accounts managed
• Transactions

4. Don’t ignore smaller companies.

Everyone knows the major employers.

Far fewer people are watching smaller companies that are expanding, launching products, opening new markets or building new teams.

Pay attention to hiring signals:

• New funding
• Expansion announcements

5. Diagnose the stage where you’re losing opportunities.

For example:

100 applications - 2 interviews

Your problem may be getting through the application stage.

20 interviews - 0 offers

You may need to examine your interview answers, examples, technical knowledge,

6. The job title you search for may be hiding the jobs you want.

Companies don’t use titles consistently.

One company might call the role Talent Acquisition Specialist then another  “Recruiter” then “another”
Talent Partner, then another  “People & Talent Associate”

7. Use interviews to collect market intelligence.

An interview isn’t only an opportunity for the company to evaluate you.

Pay attention to what they’re asking, what skills keep coming up? What does the hiring manager care about What separates their strongest candidates?

8. Don’t make every cold email an ask for a job.

Sometimes the better opening is a relevant observation, useful idea, introduction, or specific reason you believe there could be a fit. The conversation can lead to the opportunity.
